description: Break any electronic product into input, processing and output sub-systems.
content_html:
Thinking in Systems

Every electronic product — from a smoke alarm to a traffic light controller — can be broken into three connected stages: an input sub-system, a processing sub-system and an output sub-system. Thinking in these three stages is one of the most powerful tools an electronics engineer has. It lets you design a complex product by solving one small section at a time.

The signal flows in one direction: from input to processing to output. Each stage has a clear role. Once you can sort components and circuits into these three categories, you can read and sketch block diagrams confidently — a skill tested on almost every past paper.

Key Fact

Every electronic system follows the same pattern: Input → Processing → Output. Input sub-systems sense the physical world. Processing sub-systems make decisions. Output sub-systems act on those decisions.

Input Sub-Systems — Sensing the World

Input sub-systems contain transducers that convert a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The specification requires you to know these sensing units:

  • Light sensor — a light-dependent resistor (LDR) whose resistance falls as light intensity increases. Used in street-light controllers and security systems.
  • Temperature sensor — an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Used in fire alarms and thermostat circuits.
  • Magnetic field sensor — a reed switch that closes when a magnet is brought close. Used in door alarms and bicycle speed sensors.
  • Pressure sensor — a force-sensitive resistor whose resistance changes with applied force. Used in electronic scales and car park barriers.
  • Moisture sensor — a pair of conducting tracks whose resistance falls when wet. Used in plant-watering monitors and rain detectors.
  • Sound sensor (microphone) — a small electret microphone that converts sound pressure waves into a varying voltage. Used in clap-activated switches and intruder alarms.
  • Rotation sensor — an encoder or potentiometer that produces a voltage or pulse train proportional to angular position or speed. Used in robotic arms and motor controllers.
  • Pulse generator — an oscillator that produces a regular stream of pulses. It acts as a timing input sub-system, providing a clock signal to processing circuits such as counters and timers. It is never placed where a sensing transducer is needed — its role is timing, not physical measurement.

Processing Sub-Systems — Making Decisions

The processing stage receives electrical signals from the inputs and decides what to do. Common processing sub-systems include:

  • Logic gates — digital circuits (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR) that combine binary signals according to a truth table.
  • Latch (bistable) — a memory element that holds its output HIGH or LOW until told to change. Useful where the output must stay on after the trigger is removed.
  • Time delay — a monostable circuit that produces a single output pulse of a set length when triggered. Used in burglar alarm hold-off timers and courtesy lights.
  • Comparator — a circuit that compares two voltages and outputs HIGH when one is larger than the other. Links the analogue sensor voltage to a digital decision.
Key Fact

Processing sub-systems operate on signals — they do not interact directly with the physical world. A comparator, logic gate, latch or timer all sit in the processing stage, never in the input or output stage.

Output Sub-Systems — Acting on Decisions

Output sub-systems convert the processed electrical signal back into something physically useful. The specification lists these output devices:

  • Lamp / LED — visual indicators. LEDs require a current-limiting resistor in series.
  • Buzzer — an audio output. Some are “active” (buzzes at a fixed frequency when supplied with DC); others are “passive” (require an AC or pulsed signal).
  • Solenoid — an electromagnetic coil that produces linear motion when energised. Used to release door locks or trigger valves.
  • Motor — converts electrical energy into continuous rotation. Used in fans, conveyor belts and robots.
  • Servo — a geared motor with a position feedback circuit, allowing controlled angular movement. Used in robotic arms and model aircraft control surfaces.
  • Loudspeaker — a high-power audio output that requires an amplifier stage between the processing circuit and the speaker coil.

Most output devices cannot be driven directly by a logic gate or comparator because they need more current than those circuits can supply. A transducer driver — typically a transistor or MOSFET switch — sits between the processing output and the device to boost current capacity.

A security light turns on when it is dark AND someone is moving nearby. Break this into three stages:

Input: Two sensors are needed — an LDR (detects darkness) and a PIR motion sensor (detects movement). Each is an input sub-system.

Processing: The light should only come on if it is dark AND movement is detected. An AND logic gate combines the two signals: output is HIGH only when both inputs are HIGH.

Output: The lamp (output device). Because the AND gate cannot supply enough current to drive the lamp directly, a transistor switch (transducer driver) is added between the gate output and the lamp.

Block diagram (left to right): [LDR sensor] → [AND gate] ← [PIR sensor] → [Transistor driver] → [Lamp]

Examiners have consistently penalised three types of error in block diagrams:

1. Mixing up stages. Putting a logic gate in the input stage or a thermistor in the output stage. Remember: transducers are always inputs; decision circuits are always processing; actuators are always outputs.

2. Inventing blocks not needed by the specification. Adding a pulse generator where no timing is required (e.g. a simple light sensor to LED circuit needs no clock). Only include a block if the system description justifies it.

3. Omitting the transducer driver. When the output is a motor, relay, solenoid or lamp, a transistor or MOSFET driver is almost always required. Logic gates and comparators cannot supply the current these devices need directly.
exam_tip_html: Block diagram questions ask you to complete or design a system. Before writing anything, identify the physical quantity being sensed, then map it to the correct input transducer. Next, decide whether the processing stage needs a logic decision (AND/OR/NOT gate), a time delay (monostable) or a comparison (comparator). Finally, check whether the output device needs a transducer driver. Write the sub-system name in each box — never draw a full circuit where a block diagram is asked for. Two marks are typically awarded for correct stage identification and one for correct signal direction arrows.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All electronic systems have three stages — input (sensing), processing (decision) and output (action). Signal flows from left to right in a block diagram.
  • Input transducers include LDRs, thermistors, microphones, pressure sensors, moisture sensors and pulse generators. Each converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
  • High-current output devices (motors, lamps, solenoids) always need a transducer driver between the processing circuit and the device itself.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an input sub-system in an electronic burglar alarm?
A) A buzzer
B) A transistor switch
C) A magnetic reed switch
D) A logic gate
practice_questions.marks: C) A magnetic reed switch [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a transducer driver and give one example of a component used as one.
practice_questions.marks: Transducer driver: a circuit placed between the processing sub-system and an output device to supply the extra current the output device requires [1 mark]. Example: an npn transistor or n-channel MOSFET [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student designs a greenhouse heating system. The heater turns on when the temperature falls below a set level. Complete the block diagram by identifying a suitable sub-system for each stage:

Input stage: ___________
Processing stage: ___________
Output stage: ___________
practice_questions.marks: Input stage: NTC thermistor (temperature sensor / thermistor voltage divider) [1 mark]. Processing stage: comparator (compares sensor voltage with reference voltage) [1 mark]. Output stage: heater / heating element [1 mark]. Credit: transducer driver (transistor or MOSFET) between comparator and heater [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A designer adds a pulse generator to a simple moisture-sensor-to-buzzer circuit that has no timing requirement. Explain why this is an error in system design.
practice_questions.marks: The pulse generator provides a clock signal for timing circuits such as counters [1 mark]. A simple sensor-to-buzzer circuit requires no timing, so the block is unnecessary and would add unwanted complexity / change circuit behaviour [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Design a block diagram for an electronic system that sounds an alarm when it is both dark AND cold. Name each sub-system block and show the direction of signal flow.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two correct input transducers named (LDR for dark, NTC thermistor for cold) with correct signal flow arrows; AND gate identified as processing sub-system; buzzer as output; transistor/MOSFET transducer driver included between AND gate and buzzer. All five elements correctly named and connected.
Secure: Four of the five elements correctly identified with signal flow; minor omission (e.g. transducer driver missing) or one block mislabelled.
Developing: Two or three elements correct; AND gate or at least one correct transducer named; flow direction partially correct.
Emerging: One correct element identified; diagram incomplete or signal flow incorrect throughout.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using a block diagram approach when designing a complex electronic system such as an automated greenhouse controller. Refer to the input, processing and output stages in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both advantages and disadvantages with specific reference to all three stages. Advantages include: isolating faults to one stage without testing the whole system; allowing different engineers to work on each stage simultaneously; making signal flow clear so each stage can be specified independently. Disadvantages include: a block diagram does not show component-level detail needed for construction; interactions between stages (e.g. loading effects, current limits) are hidden; it can give false confidence that a design works when sub-system interfaces have not been verified. Justified conclusion on whether the benefits outweigh the drawbacks for the greenhouse context.
Secure: Clear evaluation of at least two advantages and one disadvantage with reference to at least two stages; conclusion present but may be brief.
Developing: Some advantages and disadvantages stated rather than evaluated; reference to stages inconsistent; conclusion limited.
Emerging: Simple points about block diagrams with little or no evaluation; stages not clearly referenced.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sub-system stage does a comparator circuit belong to?
An NTC thermistor is used as which type of sensor in an electronic system?
A transistor or MOSFET placed between the processing sub-system and a high-current output device is called a _____ driver.
In any electronic system, the signal flows from the input stage through the _____ stage to the output stage.
Match each component to its correct sub-system stage:

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three stages of any electronic system, in order?
What does an input transducer do?
flashcard_questions.a: Converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sensor has a resistance that falls when light intensity increases?
Which sensor has a resistance that falls as temperature rises?
What role does a pulse generator play in an electronic system?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides a regular clock signal for timing circuits; it is an input sub-system.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a logic gate not usually drive a motor or solenoid directly?
flashcard_questions.a: Logic gates cannot supply enough current; a transducer driver is needed.
A transistor or MOSFET switch that boosts current between the processing circuit and a high-current output device.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two processing sub-system types from the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: logic gate, latch (bistable), time delay (monostable), comparator.

flashcard_questions.q: A reed switch closes when a magnet is nearby. Which physical quantity does it sense?
In a block diagram, in which direction does signal flow?
flashcard_questions.a: Left to right, from input to processing to output.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of output device converts electrical energy into continuous rotation?
Which output device requires a current-limiting resistor connected in series?

glossary_terms.definition: A sub-system that detects a physical quantity such as light, temperature or sound and converts it into an electrical signal.
A diagram that represents an electronic system using labelled boxes for each sub-system, connected by arrows showing signal flow.
A component that converts a physical quantity (light, heat, sound, pressure) into an electrical signal.
A circuit (transistor or MOSFET switch) placed between the processing sub-system and a high-current output device to provide the extra current needed.
